clue.text: "Beowulf" is one early poem in canon's origins

indicators.note: origins are where things begin, so take the opening letter of each word

parts.note: initial letters of these four words

explanation.surface: A literary note placing Beowulf among the oldest poems of the English canon.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: the first letters spell the answer while the sentence describes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Beowulf is an example of a long heroic narrative poem, the genre this word names.

clue.text: The "Greatest" — but with no function in the ring?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: unsurpassed, the best of all, as Muhammad Ali styled himself

definitions.text: with no function in the ring
definitions.meaning: a boxer's corner assistant serving nobody

explanation.walkthrough: In boxing a second is the helper in a fighter's corner; one attending nobody has no job in the ring. The question mark flags this playful reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom meaning unsurpassed, the very best, so it matches being the greatest.

clue.text: Inept about Muslim ruler ensnared by good-for-nothing editor

indicators.note: something caught in a snare is trapped inside it, so these pieces go within

parts.note: a cad is a worthless rogue
c. is short for circa, about
a khan is a ruler in Central Asia

explanation.surface: An incompetent tale of a sultan trapped by a scoundrel and a newspaper editor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like a link word meaning concerning, but here it is the abbreviation c. for circa. A khan was a ruler in Central Asia and Mughal India.
explanation.definitionFit: Cack-handed is informal British for clumsy or incompetent, so it matches inept.

clue.text: Interminable disorder for German Chancellor given 50% discount by old Austrian hypnotist

indicators.note: without an end, so the final letter is cut off
a half-price discount keeps only half of the surname

parts.note: mess with its last letter removed
the first half of Angela Merkel's surname

explanation.surface: A political jibe pairing a German leader's endless chaos with a cut-price Viennese mesmerist.
explanation.walkthrough: Franz Mesmer, the eighteenth-century doctor behind 'mesmerism', gives us the verb mesmerise.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Anton Mesmer was an Austrian-born physician famous for animal magnetism, an early form of hypnosis.

clue.text: Sluggish older relative given time to attend lads' party

indicators.note: attending means following along behind, so these letters come after the party

parts.note: a stag party is a groom's night out with his friends before the wedding

explanation.surface: A slow-moving granny pops along to a stag night for a while.
explanation.definitionFit: Stagnant water does not flow, and figuratively it means sluggish or inactive.

clue.text: Heart's gone astray in balls-up with the mortuary table

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its centre, and losing it drops the middle letter
letters gone astray have wandered out of their proper order

parts.note: the middle letter of balls is removed

explanation.surface: A mortuary mix-up where something vital has gone missing from the table.
explanation.definitionFit: A slab is the flat stone or metal table on which corpses are laid in a morgue.

clue.text: Unfounded claim to expertise laid bare by doubt about a fashion designer's initials

indicators.note: going about something means surrounding it on both sides

explanation.surface: A fraudster's pretensions exposed when someone doubts a designer label's letters.
explanation.walkthrough: Calvin Klein's brand is known simply by its initials, a common crossword source of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Quackery is the practice of a charlatan, especially falsely claiming medical skill.

clue.text: See 13 across
Shut up about little book by boy being common

indicators.note: the confining word goes around the rest

parts.note: pent means confined, as in pent-up

explanation.surface: Someone told to keep quiet over a pamphlet and a lad, which apparently happens a lot.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'about' does double duty, giving a piece of its own and also signalling the outer word going around the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Something prevalent is widespread or usual, which is what common means here.

clue.text: Sportsman noted for scoring entertains posh girl

indicators.note: a host who entertains takes a guest inside

parts.note: Brian Lara, the West Indies batsman famous for record-breaking innings
U means upper-class in British slang

explanation.surface: A prolific scorer charming a well-to-do young woman, in both senses.
explanation.walkthrough: U goes inside LARA.
explanation.definitionFit: Laura is a female first name, which crosswords define simply as a girl.

clue.text: Block preventing movement of Fischer's fourth pawn

indicators.note: the ordinal tells us to take just letter number four

parts.note: to hock something is to pawn it

explanation.surface: A chess note: Bobby Fischer's fourth pawn blocks the opponent's advance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pawn' is the verb, to pledge goods at a pawnbroker, not a chess piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A chock is a wedge put against a wheel to stop it from rolling.

clue.text: Corrupt Mugabe has half blacks' riches

indicators.note: only one of the two halves survives, the other is dropped
corrupted things are twisted from their proper form

explanation.surface: A jibe at Zimbabwe's corrupt former president pocketing half his citizens' wealth.
explanation.definitionFit: Megabucks is slang for a huge amount of money, i.e. great wealth.

clue.text: Thatch will never look right on them

definitions.text: Thatch will never look right on them

parts.note: surface reading: the straw roof of a country cottage

parts.words: will never look right on them
parts.note: setter's reading: thatch as slang for a mop on the head, and the occasions when it won't behave

explanation.walkthrough: The clue sounds like a roofer's lament, but thatch is also slang for the hair on someone's head.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names days when your hair refuses to look good, and by extension days when everything goes wrong.

clue.text: Cashpoint's covered with undies!

indicators.note: in a down answer something covered has the other piece placed on top of it

parts.note: a bra is an item of underwear
split after cash: point is a compass point, S, and the apostrophe-s is read as another S

explanation.surface: A cash machine draped in underwear, a scene of comic vandalism.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition hides inside 'Cashpoint's', a British word for an ATM; it splits as cash plus point's.
explanation.definitionFit: Brass is northern British slang for money, as in 'where there's muck there's brass'.

clue.text: Lives by double dose of drug in conjunction with liqueur

definitions.note: aniseed is the flavouring of such liqueurs rather than a liqueur itself

indicators.note: the material goes inside the following word
placed beside, so the next pieces sit alongside

explanation.surface: A warning about mixing a drug, taken twice, with a strong after-dinner drink.
explanation.walkthrough: IS and EE go inside AND. Aniseed flavours drinks like anisette and ouzo, which is how it stands for a liqueur.
explanation.definitionFit: Aniseed is the seed whose flavour defines anise liqueurs, a loose stand-in for the drink.

clue.text: "I five, innit?" Confused? It's a basic verbal form!

indicators.note: a confused jumble has its letters muddled up

parts.note: the ten letters of the quoted phrase

explanation.surface: A grammar teacher despairing at slangy speech mangling the basics of verbs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Innit' is British slang for 'isn't it'.
explanation.definitionFit: The infinitive is the base form of a verb, such as 'to go', not inflected for person or tense.

clue.text: Artist in ordure reeks!

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the run of letters that follows

explanation.surface: An art critic's unkind verdict that a painter's work smells of dung.
explanation.definitionFit: Albrecht Dürer was a German Renaissance painter and engraver.

clue.text: Change for the better at midday?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: improve, as with a revised law
second meaning, cryptically: the close of the morning, a.m. end

explanation.walkthrough: Split it as A.M. END: midday is when the a.m. ends. The question mark flags the playful second reading.
explanation.definitionFit: To amend a text or law is to correct or improve it.

clue.text: Weeping, topless, captivating young woman exposes agent

indicators.note: with no top, the first letter is removed
captivating means holding captive, enclosing

explanation.surface: A risqué spy-story scene: a tearful, topless femme fatale unmasks a secret agent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topless' and 'young woman' paint a racy picture, but topless just strips a first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An emissary is a representative sent on a mission, an agent acting for someone.

clue.text: Sexy photo's centrepiece

indicators.note: a centrepiece is the middle part, so only the core letters are kept

parts.note: the middle three letters of photo

explanation.surface: A racy picture forming the heart of a display.
explanation.definitionFit: Hot is informal for sexually attractive.

clue.text: Expression of discomfort not entirely suppressed by large gathering at such a feast

indicators.note: incomplete, so the final letter is dropped
held down within something else, so these letters go inside

explanation.surface: A guest stifling a groan of indigestion at a big outdoor banquet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'such a feast' refers back to the surface; a hog roast is a pig spit-roasted whole for a crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: A hog roast is a party where a whole pig is roasted, a kind of feast.

clue.text: Back in Surrey, officials lobby

indicators.note: going back means reading from right to left
the letters lie within the words that follow

explanation.surface: Council officials back in Surrey lobbying for something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lobby' looks like a verb about officials pressing their case, but it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A foyer is the entrance hall of a theatre or hotel, i.e. a lobby.

clue.text: Turn up after appeal for quiet during lively party

indicators.note: placing these letters after the others fixes the order

parts.note: in meaning within a time, as in 'in the night'
to dig is to turn up soil

explanation.surface: Someone shows up after a plea for hush during a noisy party.
explanation.definitionFit: A shindig is informal for a big, noisy celebration.

clue.text: North African keeps small creature in check

indicators.note: keeping something means holding it within

parts.note: a Moor is from North Africa
a nit is a louse egg

explanation.surface: A North African keeping a tiny animal under control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Creature in check' looks like part of one phrase, but 'in' is only the link to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To monitor something is to keep it under observation, to check on it.

clue.text: Old English writer's bad Latin story missing two leading characters

indicators.note: losing the front two letters, the ones that lead

parts.note: mal- is the Latin-derived root for bad, as in malus
story without its first two letters

explanation.surface: A literary critic panning an old English author's poor tale in Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Thomas Malory wrote Le Morte d'Arthur in fifteenth-century England.

clue.text: See 2
Purgative for powerless clergyman gripped by wind

indicators.note: power abbreviates to one letter, which is removed
held inside the grip of the other word

parts.note: pastor without P, the abbreviation for power

explanation.surface: A laxative prescribed for a feeble vicar suffering from flatulence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wind' reads as flatulence, but it is the verb, rhyming with 'find'.
explanation.definitionFit: Castor oil is a traditional laxative, taken to purge the bowels.

clue.text: Groom's small measure of comfort, swapping sport for love

indicators.note: one item is taken out and another slotted into its place

explanation.surface: A bridegroom finds a little solace by giving up his sport for romance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Groom' looks like a bridegroom, but it is the verb, to tidy hair.
explanation.definitionFit: To comb hair or a horse's coat is to groom it.

clue.text: Declared eggs finished

indicators.note: something declared is said out loud, so the sound matters

explanation.surface: A cook announcing the eggs are done.
explanation.walkthrough: In non-rhotic British speech, ova and over sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Over means ended or completed, as in 'the game is over'.

clue.text: Colour of Spike, having consumed gallons

indicators.note: consuming means taking inside

parts.note: a tine is a prong or spike

explanation.surface: Someone called Spike turns a shade after drinking gallons.
explanation.walkthrough: G goes inside TINE. 'Spike' looks like a name, but it is a prong.
explanation.definitionFit: A tinge is a slight shade of colour, and as a verb, to colour faintly.

clue.text: Get deservedly close, top to bottom

indicators.note: in a down entry the first letter is moved to the end

explanation.surface: Coming close to deserving the top spot rather than the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: To earn something is to gain it as a reward one merits.

clue.text: Religious instruction a no-no in wedding for Mrs Simpson

indicators.note: something forbidden in a place is not allowed there, so it is removed

parts.note: the abbreviation used for RE lessons in British schools

explanation.surface: A religious lesson being banned at a wedding, as though for Wallis Simpson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mrs Simpson' suggests Wallis Simpson, whose marriage to Edward VIII was the scandal, but it is Homer's wife.
explanation.definitionFit: Marge Simpson is the cartoon mother in The Simpsons, wife of Homer.

clue.text: Old scribe of Spenser's first chapter split with the Faerie Queene!

indicators.note: first means only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: Elizabeth Regina, the queen Spenser's poem honours

explanation.surface: An old copyist working on Edmund Spenser's epic The Faerie Queene.
explanation.walkthrough: Spenser's Faerie Queene allegorises Elizabeth I, so it gives ER.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrivener was a professional writer or copier of documents before printing was common.
